triggered_regulations.name: Regulation #6
triggered_regulations.triggering_sentence:
SOURCE: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health: WHO Guidance | Section 07.3
Title: Development Phase: Data Protection Laws and Informed Consent

WHO supports application and enforcement of standards including data protection rules that govern how data have and will be used to train LMMs. Data protection laws are usually based on rights-based approaches and include standards for regulation of data-processing that both protect rights of individuals and establish obligations for public and private data controllers and processers. As data protection laws have been adopted in over 150 countries, they provide solid foundation for development of all AI technologies including LMMs. One requirement of data protection that should be enforced is that data are obtained and processed lawfully. This will often require provision of meaningful informed consent by data subject for use of their data for stated purpose. Any further processing should have its own legal basis. Pursuit of ever-larger LMMs requiring increasingly larger data sets may lead developers to ignore legal requirements.
triggered_regulations.reason: This AI system operates in the healthcare domain processing highly sensitive data types — including health data, biometric data, special category data, children's data, and personally identifiable information — across multiple jurisdictions (UK_GDPR, LK_PDPA, EU_AI_ACT, UK_MDR), which directly triggers the WHO guidance's emphasis on data protection laws governing how data is obtained and processed lawfully, particularly given the involvement of minors and rights-affecting decisions. The system's diagnostic decision support capability means that the data used to develop and operate it must have a clear, lawful legal basis with meaningful informed consent from data subjects (including appropriate guardianship consent for children), as the WHO guidance explicitly warns that the pursuit of larger datasets may lead developers to bypass these legal requirements, making rigorous data protection governance essential at every phase of this system's development and deployment.

triggered_regulations.name: Regulation #4
triggered_regulations.triggering_sentence:
SOURCE: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights | Section 7.4
Title: Definition: Sensitive Data

Data and metadata are sensitive if they pertain to an individual in a sensitive domain; are generated by technologies used in a sensitive domain; can be used to infer data from a sensitive domain or sensitive data about an individual (such as disability-related data, genomic data, biometric data, behavioral data, geolocation data, data related to interaction with the criminal justice system, relationship history and legal status such as custody and divorce information, and home, work, or school environmental data); or have the reasonable potential to be used in ways that are likely to expose individuals to meaningful harm, such as a loss of privacy or financial harm due to identity theft. Data and metadata generated by or about those who are not yet legal adults is also sensitive.
triggered_regulations.reason: The AI system processes multiple categories of sensitive data — including health data, biometric data, special category data, and children's data — all of which fall squarely within the definition of sensitive data under Regulation #4 (Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, Section 7.4), as these data types pertain to individuals in a sensitive domain (healthcare), can be used to infer sensitive attributes, and carry a reasonable potential to expose individuals to meaningful harm such as loss of privacy. Furthermore, the system's use of data belonging to children and minors is explicitly identified as sensitive under this regulation, and its rights-affecting diagnostic decision support capability operating across jurisdictions flagged under UK_GDPR, EU_AI_ACT, UK_MDR, and LK_PDPA further reinforces why the sensitive data definition in this regulation is directly relevant to this system's governance considerations.

triggered_regulations.name: Regulation #1
triggered_regulations.reason: The AI system processes biometric data within a healthcare diagnostic decision support context, which intersects with EU AI Act Article 5's provisions on exceptions to prohibited real-time remote biometric identification practices — a particularly sensitive area given the system's use of biometric and special category data on children and rights-affecting decisions under jurisdictions including the EU AI Act. The regulation's enumerated exceptions (e.g., crime victim search, imminent safety threats, national security) are relevant as reference points because the system's biometric data processing capabilities and high-risk profile — spanning health, biometric, and children's data — place it in a domain where any biometric identification functionality would need to be carefully scoped against these narrow permissible use cases to avoid falling under prohibited practices.

triggered_regulations.name: Regulation #5
triggered_regulations.triggering_sentence:
SOURCE: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (UK) | Section 5.1.13
Title: Societal Harms: Data Protection Law Reform for AI

Data is foundation for modelling, training, and developing AI systems. It is critical to respect relevant individual rights and data protection principles should be complied with when processing personal data in AI systems. The UK's data protection framework, being reformed through Data Protection and Digital Information Bill (DPDI), will complement pro-innovation, proportionate, and context-based approach to regulating AI. Current rules on automated decision-making are confusing and complex, undermining confidence to develop and use innovative technologies. The DPDI Bill will expand lawful bases on which solely automated decisions that have significant effects on individuals can take place and provide boost in confidence to organizations looking to use technologies responsibly. It will continue to ensure data subject rights are protected with safeguards in place, including providing information on decisions, opportunity to make representations, and ability to request human intervention or contest decisions.
triggered_regulations.reason: This AI system operates in the healthcare domain processing highly sensitive data categories — including health data, biometric data, special category data, children's data, and personally identifiable information — under jurisdictions such as UK_GDPR and EU_AI_ACT, making data protection principles and individual rights directly relevant as outlined in Regulation #5, which addresses societal harms arising from improper data handling in AI systems. Furthermore, the system's diagnostic decision support capability is rights-affecting and involves automated decision-making that can have significant effects on individuals (including children/minors), directly engaging the concerns raised in the regulation regarding the need for safeguards such as transparency about decisions, the ability to make representations, and the option to request human intervention under the evolving UK data protection framework (DPDI Bill).

required_controls.description: Human oversight plan — when and how humans intervene
Ownership and accountability — named responsible role
Documented purpose and scope — intended use and limits
Data minimisation — only necessary data collected

recommendations.action: Establish a fully documented Human Oversight Framework covering real-time intervention mechanisms, override/disagreement procedures, escalation pathways (including radiologist unavailability), emergency/urgent scenario protocols, and ongoing oversight effectiveness monitoring. This must be supported by a formal policy document — not a single-sentence submission.
recommendations.why: The system operates in a high-risk healthcare domain involving special category data and rights-affecting decisions for children/minors. GOV-05 scored 20/100 with no real-time intervention mechanism, no override process, no fallback procedure, and no edge-case coverage. At Industrial assurance level, Regulation #6 and Regulation #1 require robust, documented human control mechanisms for high-risk AI systems. Low model interpretability further amplifies the need for meaningful human oversight at every operational stage.

recommendations.action: Define, document, and implement a comprehensive Incident Response Plan covering all incident types (false negatives, false positives, cybersecurity breaches, prompt injection, data integrity failures, system outages), with defined SLAs for each escalation step, containment/investigation/remediation/post-incident review stages, patient safety communication procedures, and evidence of plan testing or tabletop exercises.
recommendations.why: GOV-06 scored 20/100 and covers only false negative incidents, leaving the system exposed to unmanaged cybersecurity, data integrity, and clinical harm scenarios. Given the presence of special category data, children/minors, and a high-risk domain, Regulation #4 and Regulation #6 require comprehensive incident detection, logging, triage, and escalation procedures. The absence of tested response plans at Industrial assurance level represents a critical operational and regulatory gap.

recommendations.action: Conduct and document a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) covering all processing activities, including primary diagnostic use, model training on health data, secondary/administrative processing, and audit use. Identify and document lawful bases under UK GDPR Article 9(2) for each processing purpose, and establish procedures for recording, managing, and withdrawing consent for both adult and paediatric patients.
recommendations.why: PRIV-02 scored 20/100 with no lawful basis identified beyond paediatric parental consent, no adult consent mechanism, no DPIA, and no transparency obligations addressed. Processing special category health data for children/minors without a documented lawful basis for each purpose is a fundamental gap. Regulation #5 and Regulation #1 require explicit lawful basis documentation and DPIAs for high-risk processing of sensitive data at Industrial assurance level.

recommendations.action: Define and document all human oversight roles beyond consultant radiologists — including clinical leads, AI governance officers, and safety monitors — with explicit accountability structures, role descriptions, and governance frameworks. Ensure the 4-hour training programme is expanded to explicitly cover oversight duties, escalation responsibilities, human-in-the-loop obligations, and is supplemented by periodic refresher training with attendance records.
recommendations.why: HUMO-01 scored 20/100 with no defined oversight roles, no accountability structure, and no evidence that training covers oversight-specific duties. In a high-risk domain with low model interpretability and rights-affecting decisions for children/minors, Regulation #6 and Regulation #1 require clearly assigned, competency-maintained human oversight roles. Undefined accountability at Industrial assurance level creates systemic governance failure risk.

recommendations.action: Implement a patient and stakeholder transparency mechanism that informs patients (and guardians of minors) that AI is being used in their diagnosis, explains the role of the AI system, and provides accessible information about their rights. This must be documented in a formal transparency notice or patient-facing communication policy.
recommendations.why: GOV-05 identifies the absence of any patient transparency mechanism as a gap. The system processes special category data for children/minors in a rights-affecting context. Regulation #5 and Regulation #1 require that data subjects are informed of AI-assisted processing. Failure to disclose AI use in clinical diagnosis undermines informed consent and patient autonomy, particularly for vulnerable populations.

recommendations.action: Establish a centralised audit logging and oversight decision recording system that captures all AI outputs, radiologist override decisions, escalation events, and incident notifications. Logs must be tamper-evident, time-stamped, and retained in accordance with applicable regulatory retention periods to support post-release audit compliance.
recommendations.why: GOV-05 explicitly identifies the absence of logging and auditing of oversight decisions as a gap. At Industrial assurance level, Regulation #4 and Regulation #6 require traceability of AI-assisted decisions, particularly in high-risk healthcare settings involving special category data and children/minors. Low model interpretability makes post-hoc audit logs an essential compensating control.

recommendations.action: Develop and implement a model interpretability and explainability strategy appropriate for the Industrial assurance level, including documentation of model limitations, confidence thresholds, and guidance for radiologists on how to critically evaluate and contextualise AI outputs — particularly for paediatric cases.
recommendations.why: Low model interpretability is a top risk driver. In a high-risk healthcare domain with rights-affecting decisions for children/minors, Regulation #1 and Regulation #6 require that AI outputs can be understood and critically evaluated by human overseers. HUMO-01 gaps confirm that training does not currently address critical evaluation of AI outputs, compounding interpretability risk.

recommendations.action: Produce and submit formal supporting evidence artefacts for all four Not_Ready controls (GOV-05, GOV-06, HUMO-01, PRIV-02), replacing all text-only submissions with policy documents, procedural records, training materials, role definitions, and implementation evidence prior to the next design review cycle.
recommendations.why: All four controls scored 20/100 and were submitted as text-only with no supporting documentation. At Industrial assurance level, Regulation #4 and Regulation #6 require substantive, verifiable evidence of control implementation — not assertions. The absence of artefacts across governance, oversight, incident response, and privacy controls collectively indicates systemic documentation immaturity that must be remediated before any assurance assessment can proceed.
